{{Short description|Concept in mathematics}}
In mathematics, given an [[Group-scheme action|action]] <math>\sigma: G \times_S X \to X</math> of a [[group scheme]] ''G'' on a scheme ''X'' over a base scheme ''S'',<!-- In the equivariant setting, it is necessary to work with stacks such as algebraic spaces rather than just schemes.--> an '''equivariant sheaf''' ''F'' on ''X'' is a sheaf of [[sheaf of modules|<math>\mathcal{O}_X</math>-modules]] together with the isomorphism of <math>\mathcal{O}_{G \times_S X}</math>-modules

:<math>\phi: \sigma^* F \xrightarrow{\simeq} p_2^*F</math> &nbsp;

that satisfies the cocycle condition:<ref>{{harvnb|MFK|1994|loc=Ch 1. § 3. Definition 1.6.}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Gaitsgory|2005|loc=§ 6.}}</ref> writing ''m'' for multiplication,
:<math>p_{23}^* \phi \circ (1_G \times \sigma)^* \phi = (m \times 1_X)^* \phi</math>.

== Notes on the definition ==
On the stalk level, the cocycle condition says that the isomorphism <math>F_{gh \cdot x} \simeq F_x</math> is the same as the composition <math>F_{g \cdot h \cdot x} \simeq F_{h \cdot x} \simeq F_x</math>; i.e., the associativity of the group action. The condition that the unit of the group acts as the identity is also a consequence: apply <math>(e \times e \times 1)^*, e: S \to G</math> to both sides to get <math>(e \times 1)^* \phi \circ (e \times 1)^* \phi = (e \times 1)^* \phi</math> and so <math>(e \times 1)^* \phi</math> is the identity.

Note that <math>\phi</math> is an additional data; it is "a lift" of the action of ''G'' on ''X'' to the sheaf ''F''. Moreover, when ''G'' is a connected [[algebraic group]],  ''F'' an [[invertible sheaf]] and ''X'' is reduced, the cocycle condition is automatic: any isomorphism <math>\sigma^* F \simeq p_2^* F</math> automatically satisfies the cocycle condition.<ref>{{harvnb|MFK|1994|loc=end of the proof of Ch. 1, § 3., Proposition 1.5.}}</ref>

If the action of ''G'' is free, then the notion of an equivariant sheaf simplifies to a sheaf on the quotient ''X''/''G'', because of the [[descent along torsors]].

By [[Yoneda's lemma]], to give the structure of an equivariant sheaf to an <math>\mathcal{O}_X</math>-module ''F'' is the same as to give group homomorphisms for rings ''R'' over <math>S</math>,
:<math>G(R) \to \operatorname{Aut}(X \times_S \operatorname{Spec}R, F \otimes_S R)</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Thomason|1987|loc=§ 1.2.}}</ref>

There is also a definition of equivariant sheaves in terms of [[simplicial sheaves]]. Alternatively, one can define an equivariant sheaf to be an [[equivariant object]] in the [[category (mathematics)|category]] of, say, [[coherent sheaf|coherent sheaves]].

== Linearized line bundles ==
A structure of an equivariant sheaf on an invertible sheaf or a line bundle is also called a '''linearization'''.

Let ''X'' be a [[complete variety]] over an algebraically closed field acted by a connected [[reductive group]] ''G'' and ''L'' an invertible sheaf on it. If ''X'' is normal, then some tensor power <math>L^n</math> of ''L'' is linearizable.<ref>{{harvnb|MFK|1994|loc=Ch 1. § 3. Corollary 1.6.}}</ref>

Also, if ''L'' is very ample and linearized, then there is a ''G''-linear closed immersion from ''X'' to <math>\mathbf{P}^N</math> such that <math>\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}^N}(1)</math> is linearized and the linearization on ''L'' is induced by that of <math>\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{P}^N}(1)</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|MFK|1994|loc=Ch 1. § 3. Proposition 1.7.}}</ref>

Tensor products and the inverses of linearized invertible sheaves are again linearized in the natural way. Thus, the isomorphism classes of the linearized invertible sheaves on a scheme ''X'' form an [[abelian group]]. There is a homomorphism to the [[Picard group]] of ''X'' which forgets the linearization; this homomorphism is neither injective nor surjective in general, and its kernel can be identified with the isomorphism classes of linearizations of the trivial line bundle. 

See Example 2.16 of [https://www-fourier.ujf-grenoble.fr/~mbrion/linearization] for an example of a variety for which most line bundles are not linearizable.

== Dual action on sections of equivariant sheaves ==
Given an algebraic group ''G'' and a ''G''-equivariant sheaf ''F'' on ''X'' over a field ''k'', let <math>V =\Gamma(X, F)</math> be the space of global sections. It then admits the structure of a ''G''-module; i.e., ''V'' is a [[linear representation]] of ''G'' as follows. Writing <math>\sigma: G \times X \to X</math> for the group action, for each ''g'' in ''G'' and ''v'' in ''V'', let
:<math>\pi(g)v = (\varphi \circ \sigma^*)(v)(g^{-1})</math>
where <math>\sigma^*: V \to \Gamma(G \times X, \sigma^* F)</math> and <math>\varphi: \Gamma(G \times X, \sigma^* F) \overset{\sim}\to \Gamma(G \times X, p_2^* F) = k[G] \otimes_k V</math> is the isomorphism given by the equivariant-sheaf structure on ''F''. The cocycle condition then ensures that <math>\pi: G \to GL(V)</math> is a group homomorphism (i.e., <math>\pi</math> is a representation.)

'''Example''': take <math>X = G, F = \mathcal{O}_G</math> and <math>\sigma=</math> the action of ''G'' on itself. Then <math>V = k[G]</math>, <math>(\varphi \circ \sigma^*)(f)(g, h) = f(gh)</math> and
:<math>(\pi(g)f)(h) = f(g^{-1} h)</math>,
meaning <math>\pi</math> is the [[left regular representation]] of ''G''.

The representation <math>\pi</math> defined above is a [[rational representation]]: for each vector ''v'' in ''V'', there is a finite-dimensional ''G''-submodule of ''V'' that contains ''v''.<ref>{{harvnb|MFK|1994|loc=Ch. 1. § 1. the lemma just after Definition 1.3.}}</ref>

== Equivariant vector bundle ==
A definition is simpler for a vector bundle (i.e., a variety corresponding to a [[locally free sheaf]] of constant rank). We say a vector bundle ''E'' on an [[algebraic variety]] ''X'' acted by an algebraic group ''G'' is ''equivariant'' if ''G'' acts fiberwise: i.e., <math>g: E_x \to E_{gx}</math> is a "linear" isomorphism of vector spaces.<ref>If ''E'' is viewed as a sheaf, then ''g'' needs to be replaced by <math>g^{-1}</math>.</ref> In other words, an equivariant vector bundle is a pair consisting of a vector bundle and the lifting of the action <math>G \times X \to X</math> to that of <math>G \times E \to E</math> so that the projection <math>E \to X</math> is equivariant.

Just like in the non-equivariant setting, one can define an [[equivariant characteristic class]] of an equivariant vector bundle.

== Examples ==
* The [[tangent bundle]] of a manifold or a smooth variety is an equivariant vector bundle.
* The sheaf of [[equivariant differential form]]s.
* Let ''G'' be a semisimple algebraic group, and ''λ:H→'''''C''' a character on a maximal torus ''H''. It extends to a Borel subgroup ''λ:B→'''''C''', giving a one dimensional representation ''W<sub>λ</sub>'' of ''B''. Then ''GxW<sub>λ</sub>'' is a trivial vector bundle over ''G'' on which ''B'' acts. The quotient ''L<sub>λ</sub>=Gx<sub>B</sub>W<sub>λ</sub>'' by the action of ''B'' is a line bundle over the flag variety ''G/B''. Note that ''G→G/B'' is a ''B'' bundle, so this is just an example of the associated bundle construction. The [[Borel–Weil–Bott theorem]] says that all representations of ''G'' arise as the cohomologies of such line bundles.
* If ''X=Spec(A)'' is an affine scheme, a [[group-scheme action|'''G'''<sub>m</sub>-action]] on ''X'' is the same thing as a '''Z''' [[graded ring|grading]] on ''A''. Similarly, a '''G'''<sub>m</sub> equivariant quasicoherent sheaf on ''X'' is the same thing as a '''Z''' graded ''A'' module.{{fact|date=September 2019}}
